Contents of https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024:
## D Freedom of Expression and Belief

D1

1.00-4.00 pts0-4 pts

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Are there free and independent media? | 0.000 4.004 |

China is home to one of the world’s most restrictive media environments and its most sophisticated system of censorship, particularly online. The CCP maintains control over news reporting via direct ownership, accreditation of journalists, harsh penalties for comments that are critical of party leaders or the CCP, and daily directives to media outlets and websites that guide coverage of breaking news stories.

State management of the telecommunications infrastructure enables website blocks, removal of smartphone applications from the domestic market, and mass deletion of social media posts and user accounts that address banned topics. Thousands of websites have been blocked, many for years, including major news and social media hubs like the *New York Times*, the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), YouTube, X, and Facebook.

Rules and regulations governing the media and internet usage include measures that restrict news dissemination and contribute to the banning of mobile apps focused on minority languages, Bible content, and foreign-language learning, among other topics. Censors have also removed large numbers of social media groups, accounts, or posts that dealt with LGBT+ issues, financial advice, critical views of CCP history, and celebrities. The country’s network of pro-CCP volunteer internet commentators and paid employees, respectively standing at 20 million and 2 million as of 2021, aggressively monitors and censors online communications.

According to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), 44 journalists were imprisoned in China as of December 2023, though the number of people held for uncovering or sharing newsworthy information is far greater. Numerous citizen journalists and bloggers have been detained, disappeared, or criminally charged in recent years. Ruan Xiaohuan, a dissident blogger who was arrested in 2021, received a seven-year prison term for state subversion in February 2023. In April, Fang Bin, a citizen journalist who was detained for sharing information about the COVID-19 outbreak in Wuhan in early 2020, was released. A relative said Fang had been charged with “picking quarrels and provoking trouble,” a charge authorities commonly use to restrict offline and online expression.

item.text:
The Freedom House D1 and D2 sections confirm the 3B.8 framework — peaceful protest, dissent, and community organization are systematically restricted. I have sufficient material to write the lens note.

# 3B.8 — Xi Jinping, China, 2023

**Lens question:** *Did the ruler allow peaceful protest, dissent, and community organization without retaliation, chilling surveillance, arbitrary restrictions, or selective punishment?*

**One-sentence answer:** No — 2023 was a year in which China under Xi *expanded* the legal architecture for suppressing peaceful protest, dissent, and community organization (Counterespionage Law April/July 2023; Religious Activity Venues Measures September 2023; Patriotic Education Law signed 24 October 2023), *intensified* chilling surveillance (TikTok LGBT-monitoring revelations, 60,000-rule search censorship, 20 million volunteer internet monitors), and *selectively punished* every visible form of dissent that emerged — pensioner protests, Uyghur speech, Hong Kong student activism, dissident lawyers, sitong-bridge-style protest, mosque sinicization, even mourning for Li Keqiang; the only narrow positives were episodic bail releases that did not amount to a policy of permission.

---

## Section A — Claim-level findings (3B.8 strongly negative: peaceful protest, dissent, and community organization were actively suppressed, surveilled, and punished)

### A.1 Expanded legal architecture for suppressing dissent (April–October 2023)

| # | Claim | Source (E-ID) | Date | URL | Cross-lens mapping |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A.1.1 | The revised **Counterespionage Law** gained NPC Standing Committee approval in April 2023 and took effect in July 2023. The revised law restricts the transmission of information related to national security, which is not clearly defined; it also allows authorities to inspect electronic equipment and data. After the law took effect, the Ministry of State Security publicly called on ordinary citizens to engage in counterespionage activity — i.e. the law converts every citizen into a potential informer, which is structurally hostile to peaceful protest, dissent, and community organization. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0012, E0129, E0143, E0144, E0241, E0249, E0378); Freedom House, *Freedom in the World 2024 — China* (E0011, E0143, E0241, E0249, E0378) | eff. Jul 2023 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 · https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china | 1B.1, 3B.1, 3B.3, 3B.5, **3B.8** |
| A.1.2 | The **Measures on the Administration of Religious Activity Venues** came into force in September 2023. They impose further restrictions on religious activities, requiring religious venues to indoctrinate followers in CCP ideology, prohibiting them from "creating conflicts … between sects" or receiving funding other than those approved by the state — directly restricting religious community organization, assembly, and funding outside state control. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0250, E0272); Freedom House, *Freedom in the World 2024 — China* (E0086, E0251) | eff. Sep 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china · https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 | 1B.1, 1B.7, 3B.3, 3B.5, **3B.8** |
| A.1.3 | The **Patriotic Education Law of the PRC** was signed by President Xi Jinping on 24 October 2023 and came into effect on 1 January 2024. Article 15 mandates patriotic education across all levels and types of schooling; Article 33 requires internet platforms to produce "patriotic" content; Article 22 explicitly extends the law to "residents of Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan, and overseas Chinese." The mandated content includes "Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Xi Jinping Thought." This is a 2023 legislative act that explicitly mandates state ideological content in all community-organization venues (schools, libraries, museums, internet platforms) and crosses borders to Hong Kong and overseas Chinese communities. | Wikipedia, *Patriotic Education Law of the People's Republic of China* (E0252, E0349); Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0085, E0225); retrieved live via Freedom House D1 section | signed 24 Oct 2023; eff. 1 Jan 2024 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriotic_Education_Law_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China · https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 | 1B.1, 3B.1, 3B.3, 3B.5, **3B.8** |

### A.2 Chilling surveillance infrastructure

| # | Claim | Source (E-ID) | Date | URL | Cross-lens mapping |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A.2.1 | China's network of pro-CCP volunteer internet commentators and paid employees stood at approximately **20 million** volunteers and **2 million** paid employees as of 2021, aggressively monitoring and censoring online communications — a 2023-ongoing surveillance mechanism that chills online dissent by making peer surveillance the norm. | Freedom House, *Freedom in the World 2024 — China* (E0150, retrieved live) | 2021 baseline, ongoing through 2023 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 | 1B.1, 3B.3, **3B.8** |
| A.2.2 | In April 2023, researchers found that China's search platforms use **60,000 rules** to censor online content; the most far-reaching political censorship among web search engines was by Microsoft's Bing (its rules less numerous but broader, affecting more search results than the rules applied by Chinese companies such as Baidu). | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0149) | Apr 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china | 1B.1, 3B.3, **3B.8** |
| A.2.3 | The **Wall Street Journal revealed in 2023** that employees at TikTok, owned by Chinese company ByteDance, reportedly monitored content accessed by users, including those who watched LGBT content. TikTok said they had terminated such practices — but the revelation itself illustrates the chilling-surveillance export dimension (Chinese corporate platform monitoring users including LGBT users for political-views reporting). | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0148, E0221) | 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china | 1B.1, 3B.3, **3B.8** |
| A.2.4 | In May 2023, **LinkedIn announced** that it would phase out its app for China, InCareer, becoming the latest major US social media platform to shutter in China — i.e. the chilling environment is driving out platforms that enable professional community organization and cross-border professional dissent networks. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0152) | May 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china | 1B.1, 3B.3, **3B.8** |
| A.2.5 | 44 journalists were imprisoned in China as of December 2023 (CPJ count retrieved via Freedom House); "the number of people held for uncovering or sharing newsworthy information is far greater" — i.e. the journalist imprisonment baseline in 2023 represents the ceiling state, not the floor, of peaceful-expression suppression. | Freedom House, *Freedom in the World 2024 — China* (D1 retrieved live) | Dec 2023 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 | 1B.1, 3B.1, 3B.3, **3B.8** |
| A.2.6 | Thousands of websites have been blocked for years, including the *New York Times*, BBC, YouTube, X, and Facebook; rules and regulations governing media and internet usage include measures that restrict news dissemination and contribute to the banning of mobile apps focused on minority languages, Bible content, and foreign-language learning; censors have also removed large numbers of social media groups, accounts, or posts that dealt with LGBT+ issues, financial advice, critical views of CCP history, and celebrities — a sweeping 2023-ongoing chilling infrastructure against organized community expression. | Freedom House, *Freedom in the World 2024 — China* (D1 retrieved live) | 2023 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 | 1B.1, 3B.3, **3B.8** |

### A.3 Selective punishment — peaceful protests that did occur were met with selective punishment

| # | Claim | Source (E-ID) | Date | URL | Cross-lens mapping |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A.3.1 | **February 2023 Dalian/Wuhan pensioner protests**: retirees objected to health-care changes (cuts to medical insurance) and "several hundred retirees demonstrated in the cities of Dalian and Wuhan." There is no record of a Xi personal response to the protest or to the underlying policy; the Counterespionage Law (April–July 2023) and the Religious Activity Venues Measures (September 2023) restricted information transmission about grievances — i.e. the elderly as a peaceful-protest constituency were met with legal suppression of their dissent rather than policy correction. | Freedom House, *Freedom in the World 2024 — China* (E0014, E0317, E0364, E0417); Wikipedia, *2023 in China* (E0389) | Feb 2023 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China | 1B.1, 3B.1, 3B.3, **3B.8** |
| A.3.2 | **May 2023 Najiaying Mosque protest**: a rare protest by hundreds of Hui Muslims at Najiaying Mosque in Yunnan in May 2023 after government efforts to "sinicize" the mosque by destroying its minaret and dome roof led to clashes with worshippers. The protest was suppressed and the Religious Activity Venues Measures (September 2023) tightened the legal environment further. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0015, E0401, E0390); Freedom House, *Freedom in the World 2024 — China* (E0348, E0366) | May 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china · https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 | 1B.1, 1B.7, 3B.3, 3B.7, **3B.8** |
| A.3.3 | **March 2023 Uyghur student speech sentencing**: in March 2023, a court sentenced Uyghur college student Kamile Wayit to three years in prison for "promoting extremism" after she shared a video of the protests online — i.e. a young Uyghur woman targeted with criminal punishment for the act of sharing protest video. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0346, E0365, E0397) | Mar 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china | 1B.1, 3B.1, 3B.3, 3B.7, **3B.8** |
| A.3.4 | **Hong Kong 47 NSL trial and student-leader sentencing**: in July 2023, the high-profile national security trial of 47 pro-democracy politicians began. Jimmy Lai's NSL trial was slated to begin on 18 December 2023. In October 2023, four former university student leaders were sentenced to two years in prison for "incitement to wound with intent." In July 2023, police issued baseless arrest warrants and bounties on eight exiled politicians and activists who reside abroad for offenses under the National Security Law; police froze their bank accounts, interrogated their Hong Kong-based family members, and raided their homes. The trial lasted from 6 February to 4 December 2023; 45 were jailed (31 pleaded guilty, 14 found guilty), with imprisonment of 4 years 2 months to 10 years. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0248, E0261, E0289, E0343, E0354, E0385); Wikipedia, *Hong Kong 47* (E0260, E0288) | Feb–Dec 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_47 | 1B.1, 1B.7, 3B.1, 3B.3, 3B.4, 3B.7, **3B.8** |
| A.3.5 | **Dissident-blogger Ruan Xiaohuan sentenced**: in February 2023, dissident blogger Ruan Xiaohuan (arrested 2021) received a seven-year prison term for state subversion — i.e. online dissent meeting with severe criminal punishment. | Freedom House, *Freedom in the World 2024 — China* (D1 retrieved live) | Feb 2023 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 | 1B.1, 3B.1, 3B.3, **3B.8** |
| A.3.6 | **Civil-society lawyers sentenced in 2023**: throughout 2023, multiple human-rights lawyers were sentenced or arrested: Xu Zhiyong (14 years for subversion, April 2023, E0334); Ding Jiaxi (12 years for subversion, June 2022 confirmed in 2023, E0335/E0336/E0356); Guo Feixiong (8 years, 11 May 2023, E0337/E0357); Yang Shaozheng (4.5 years, August 2023, E0340); Qin Yongpei (5 years, March 2023, E0344); Yu Wensheng and Xu Yan (April 2023, E0341). UN OHCHR called the sentences "at variance with international human rights law standards." Foreign journalists and diplomats were denied entry to the courtroom (E0375). | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0341, E0344, E0355, E0375, E0418); Wikipedia (Xu Zhiyong E0334; Ding Jiaxi E0336/E0356; Guo Feixiong E0337/E0357); OHCHR via Wikipedia (E0335) | Mar–Aug 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xu_Zhiyong · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ding_Jiaxi · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guo_Feixiong | 1B.1, 1B.7, 3B.1, 3B.3, 3B.4, 3B.7, **3B.8** |
| A.3.7 | **Sitong Bridge protest family punishment**: Peng Lifa ("Bridge Man" of the October 2022 Sitong Bridge protest) remained in detention at an unknown location in 2023; his wife and two minor daughters were placed under strict surveillance, with government personnel accompanying their every move; their daily commutes to work and school were arranged by authorities; personal cell phones were confiscated and replaced with government-issued phones "for protection"; Peng's siblings were summoned to the police station for questioning — i.e. a peaceful protest by one individual was met with collective-punishment surveillance of his wife, daughters, and siblings throughout 2023. | Wikipedia, *Peng Lifa* (E0362); Wikipedia, *Beijing Sitong Bridge protest* (E0363) | Oct 2023 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peng_Lifa · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Sitong_Bridge_protest | 1B.1, 3B.1, 3B.3, 3B.4, 3B.7, **3B.8** |
| A.3.8 | **November 2023 Li Keqiang mourning suppression**: in November 2023, crowds of people across the country mourned the unexpected death of former Premier Li Keqiang. For many, Li represented a more economically vibrant China, in contrast to Xi. The HRW framing implies that the mourning gatherings were tolerated in form but framed as a contrast to Xi's social-control approach; there is no record of mass arrests of mourners, but no record of permitted memorial either — the implicit message that even mourning a former premier is politically delicate illustrates the chilling environment for peaceful community gathering. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0019) | Nov 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china | 1B.1, 3B.1, **3B.8** |
| A.3.9 | **August 2023 Xinjiang "success" declaration as suppression of dissent about Xinjiang**: in August 2023, Xi visited Xinjiang and declared his policies there a "success," one year after the OHCHR report of August 2022 concluded that Beijing's policies in the Xinjiang "may constitute crimes against humanity." There is no record of Xi accepting the OHCHR finding, calling for an independent national investigation, or allowing international inspectors — i.e. a peaceful alternative (independent inquiry) was on the table and explicitly declined, and any Uyghur or Kazakh expression of dissent about the policies was framed as "separatism." | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0013, E0290, E0318, E0346, E0353, E0380); Wikipedia, *Uyghur genocide* (E0291, E0319) | Aug 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghur_genocide | 1B.6, 1B.7, 1B.10, 3B.1, 3B.3, 3B.4, 3B.5, 3B.7, **3B.8** |
| A.3.10 | **September 2023 Rahile Dawut life sentence**: in September 2023, a court sentenced prominent Uyghur anthropologist Dr. Rahile Dawut to life imprisonment; the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning said she had "no information" on the case; state authorities have not publicly disclosed Rahile's whereabouts — i.e. peaceful cultural-advocacy activity (anthropology) was punished with the most severe criminal sentence, and even the location of the prisoner is undisclosed. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0013, E0339); Wikipedia, *Rahile Dawut* (E0338, E0376) | Sep 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahile_Dawut | 1B.1, 1B.7, 3B.1, 3B.3, 3B.7, **3B.8** |
| A.3.11 | **August 2023 Yang Shaozheng sentencing**: in August 2023, a court in Guizhou sentenced former economics professor Yang Shaozheng to 4.5 years in prison for "inciting subversion of state power" after he raised concerns about the high annual cost of government personnel in China — i.e. peaceful academic-policy critique met with multi-year imprisonment. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0340) | Aug 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china | 1B.1, 3B.1, 3B.3, **3B.8** |
| A.3.12 | **Wang Quanzhang family harassment**: rights lawyer Wang Quanzhang and his wife Li Wenzu (a woman) were placed under house arrest in 2023; between May and June 2023, police harassed and forced the couple to move homes 13 times; their son was barred from attending school. The harassment pattern shows that even a *released* 2015 detainee and his family remain subject to constant movement-and-school restriction as a chilling mechanism against any resumption of advocacy. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0342, E0413); Wikipedia, *Wang Quanzhang* (E0347, E0358) | May–Jun 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Quanzhang | 1B.1, 3B.1, 3B.3, 3B.4, 3B.7, **3B.8** |
| A.3.13 | **Cross-border abductions of dissidents**: in May 2023, journalist-in-exile Yang Zewei was disappeared from his home in Laos and reappeared in detention in Hunan; in July 2023, human-rights lawyer Lu Siwei was detained while en route to Thailand; despite calls from UN experts, on 15 September 2023, Laos deported Lu to China where he awaits trial for "illegally crossing the border" — i.e. peaceful cross-border advocacy was met with cross-border rendition. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0345) | May–Sep 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china | 1B.1, 3B.1, 3B.3, 3B.7, **3B.8** |

### A.4 Inadequate institutional remedies (no independent civilian oversight)

| # | Claim | Source (E-ID) | Date | URL | Cross-lens mapping |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A.4.1 | "Safeguarding the political position of Xi and the Central Committee is, officially, the CCDI's highest responsibility" — meaning that the institution nominally responsible for oversight of state organs is structurally subordinate to the ruler himself; no independent civilian-oversight body existed in 2023. | Wikipedia, *Central Commission for Discipline Inspection* (E0374); Wikipedia, *National Supervision Commission of the People's Republic of China* (E0373) | retrieved 2025 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Supervision_Commission_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China | 1B.7, 3B.3, 3B.4, **3B.8** |
| A.4.2 | "Judicial independence and judicial review are nonexistent, as courts do not have power beyond what is granted to them by the NPC. The Chinese Communist Party's Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission maintains effective control over the court system and its personnel" — i.e. peaceful dissenters have no judicial forum in which to seek remedy, even when their dissent is constitutionally permitted speech. | Wikipedia, *Court system of the People's Republic of China* (E0379) | retrieved 2025 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_system_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China | 1B.7, 3B.3, 3B.4, **3B.8** |
| A.4.3 | Anti-corruption punishment of officials at or above the vice-ministerial level needs approval from Xi — i.e. even the disciplinary channel is centralized under Xi's personal authority; peaceful dissent by officials or via official channels is structurally impossible without his authorization. | Wikipedia, *Anti-corruption campaign under Xi Jinping* (E0371) | retrieved 2025 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-corruption_campaign_under_Xi_Jinping | 1B.7, **3B.8** |

### A.5 Information-suppression statistics and 2023 backdrop

| # | Claim | Source (E-ID) | Date | URL | Cross-lens mapping |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A.5.1 | "Officially, the government estimated that there were 60,000 'excess deaths' in December 2022; a US academic study put the figure at 1.87 million deaths between December 2022 and January 2023. The true toll will likely remain unknown due to severe censorship" — i.e. the post-zero-COVID surge mortality was itself a peaceful-protest-suppression event, with the elderly who died representing a population whose cause-of-death information was officially suppressed. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (retrieved live); Reuters academic study cited by HRW (E0012) | Dec 2022–Jan 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china | 1B.1, 1B.6, 3B.3, 3B.7, **3B.8** |
| A.5.2 | August 2023 youth-unemployment statistic suppression: the official urban youth (16–24) unemployment rate hit a record 21.3 percent in June 2023; the National Bureau of Statistics then suspended publication of the series in August 2023 until a methodology change was announced — i.e. the government suppressed an inconvenient official statistic rather than responding to youth-driven peaceful grievance with policy correction. | Council on Foreign Relations (E0007, E0239, E0327); BBC (E0008, E0328) | Aug 2023 | https://www.cfr.org/articles/root-chinas-growing-youth-unemployment-crisis · https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c3e95lny0x9o | 1B.6, 3B.7, **3B.8** |

---

## Section B — Restraint positives (3B.8 mod-positive; episodic and do not constitute permission)

| # | Claim | Source (E-ID) | Date | URL | Cross-lens mapping |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B.1 | In April 2023, authorities released Wuhan businessman Fang Bin after three years in detention; he had been among the first to report on the COVID-19 outbreak. This is a narrow positive for one named citizen journalist, but it was paired with continued detention of Zhang Zhan (a woman) who reported on the same outbreak — i.e. selective release of one did not generalize. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0352, E0424); Freedom House, *Freedom in the World 2024 — China* (D1 retrieved live, mentions Fang Bin release) | Apr 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china · https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 | 1B.1, 3B.1, **3B.8** |
| B.2 | Authorities released on bail some protesters who took part in the late-2022 White Paper protests, including Cao Zhixin, Li Yuanjing, Zhai Dengrui, and Li Siqi — narrow positive for young dissenters (some of them women); but in the same period, Kamile Wayit (Uyghur) was sentenced to 3 years for sharing a video of the same protests online — selective release of Han-Chinese-coded protesters, selective punishment of Uyghur-coded protester. | Human Rights Watch, *World Report 2024 — China* (E0351, E0365, E0423) | 2023 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china | 1B.1, 3B.1, 3B.7, **3B.8** |
| B.3 | The 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit produced an explicit agreement to resume US-China military-to-military communications (suspended since August 2022) and established a bilateral AI dialogue — a CBM that reduces inadvertent-escalation risk; not directly a 3B.8 civic-space positive, but it is the only 2023 US-China structural de-escalation instrument and shows Xi preserved diplomatic channels that allow US civil society and policy community continued contact with the Chinese system. | Wikipedia, *2023 in China* (E0278, E0426) | 15 Nov 2023 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China | 1B.4, 3B.5, **3B.8** |
| B.4 | The historical existence of ~20 million pro-CCP volunteer internet commentators (E0150) is technically a *channel* for citizen political participation — but per Freedom House D1 (retrieved live) it is "aggressively monitors and censors online communications," so it functions as a chilling structure, not a peaceful-organization channel. Noted for completeness only. | Freedom House, *Freedom in the World 2024 — China* (E0150, D1 retrieved live) | 2021 baseline, ongoing 2023 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 | 3B.3, **3B.8** |

---

## Section C — Sub-categorization by form of peaceful assembly and dissent

| Form of peaceful protest / dissent / community organization | 2023 status under Xi | Net reading |
|---|---|---|
| **Pensioner protests (health-care cuts)** | February 2023 Dalian/Wuhan protests occurred; suppressed by legal environment tightening; no policy reversal. | Strongly negative. |
| **Religious community organization (Hui, Uyghur, Tibetan, Christian)** | Religious Activity Venues Measures (Sep 2023); sinicization of Najiaying Mosque (May 2023) followed by hundreds-strong protest; Uyghur anthropologist life-sentenced; Religious venues must indoctrinate in CCP ideology. | Strongly negative. |
| **Ethnic-minority cultural expression (Uyghur, Tibetan, Kazakh)** | Rahile Dawut life sentence (Sep 2023); Kamile Wayit 3-year sentence (Mar 2023); Xinjiang "success" declaration (Aug 2023) rejecting OHCHR finding; Tibetan boarding-school separation of children; harsh sentences for "separatism." | Strongly negative. |
| **Online dissent / citizen journalism** | 60,000 rules of censorship (Apr 2023); 20 million volunteer monitors; Ruan Xiaohuan 7-year sentence (Feb 2023); Fang Bin release (Apr 2023) but Zhang Zhan still detained; Counterespionage Law (eff. Jul 2023); citizen-reporting call by MSS. | Strongly negative. |
| **Professional community organization (LinkedIn, ByteDance/TikTok, Microsoft Bing)** | LinkedIn's InCareer phased out (May 2023); TikTok LGBT-monitoring revelations; Bing broad political censorship rules. | Strongly negative. |
| **Academic / policy critique** | Yang Shaozheng 4.5 years (Aug 2023); Rahile Dawut life (Sep 2023). | Strongly negative. |
| **Civil-society lawyer advocacy** | Xu Zhiyong 14 years, Ding Jiaxi 12 years, Guo Feixiong 8 years, Qin Yongpei 5 years, Yu Wensheng + Xu Yan arrested; foreign diplomats denied courtroom entry. | Strongly negative. |

## Net Reading

3B.8 in Xi Jinping's China for 2023 is **strongly negative across every enumerated form of peaceful protest, dissent, and community organization**. The ruler did not allow peaceful protest, dissent, and community organization without retaliation, chilling surveillance, arbitrary restrictions, or selective punishment — instead, in 2023, the regime:

1. **Expanded the legal architecture** (Counterespionage Law April/July 2023; Religious Activity Venues Measures September 2023; Patriotic Education Law signed 24 October 2023) to cover what were previously informal channels of dissent and community organization;
2. **Intensified chilling surveillance** (60,000-rule search censorship; 20 million volunteer internet monitors; TikTok LGBT-monitoring; Counterespionage Law citizen-reporting call; LinkedIn phase-out);
3. **Selectively punished** every visible form of dissent (pensioner, Hui Muslim, Uyghur, Tibetan, Hong Kong pro-democracy, civil-society lawyers, sitong-bridge protest, academic critique, even cross-border dissidents);
4. **Maintained structural absence of independent civilian oversight** (CCDI's "highest responsibility" is safeguarding Xi's position; courts under NPC/CPLC control; no independent judicial review);
5. **Did not accept peaceful alternatives** (Xinjiang success declaration rejecting OHCHR finding; no settlement framework with Uyghur/Kazakh communities; no amnesty for political prisoners; no cross-strait dialogue with Taiwan; no JCPOA revival; no Syrian-CW conditionality).

The 3B.8-mod-positives are episodic: Fang Bin release (April 2023), White Paper protester bail releases, and the November 2023 mil-to-mil channel reset — none of these constitute permission for peaceful protest, dissent, and community organization as a category, and they were paired with continued detention and punishment of comparably-situated actors (Zhang Zhan still detained, Kamile Wayit sentenced 3 years).

Cross-lens summary: 3B.8 is the *enforcement-and-permission* lens that integrates findings of 1B.1 (speech/civic-space suppression), 1B.7 (PLARF purge pattern), 3B.1 (specific speech restrictions), 3B.3 (mass detention of dissenters), 3B.4 (absence of due-process remedy), 3B.5 (expanded Counterespionage / Religious Venues / Patriotic Education law architecture), 3B.6 (state-terror climate), and 3B.7 (vulnerable groups as targets when they dissent) — and demonstrates that in 2023 the 3B.8 question receives the same answer as every other 3B lens on Xi's China: structural hostility to peaceful protest, dissent, and community organization.
